newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: CRICKET-SOUTH AFRICA COMES TO TERMS WITH DEFEAT.
newsitem.headline: CRICKET-SOUTH AFRICA COMES TO TERMS WITH DEFEAT.

text.p: South Africa's sports fans and commentators have become notorious for their inability to see beyond the immediate horror of defeat since their readmission to world competition six years ago.
But Australia's two-wicket victory in the second test in Port Elizabeth on Monday, and resultant series victory, seems to have changed that. At least for now.
"Healy's six silences the choir," exclaimed the Johannesburg Star daily, referring to the winning runs and the incessant singing associated with St George's Park.

"Even if SA's batsmen can score some decent runs (in the third test) at Centurion Park, they will still be too little too late, unlike Australia's Waugh brothers and Greg Blewett who made the big scores when they really mattered," the newspaper said.
"Well done Australia, you deserve it!" wrote former Springbok captain Eddie Barlow in his weekly newspaper column.
Barlow has been critical of the South African team since being overlooked for the national coaching job two years ago.

After the test, however, he preferred to question the priorities of current coach Bob Woolmer, the wisdom of preparing a green wicket, the success of the national academy and even the lack of success of the politically sensitive development programme.
"There can be little doubt that Bob Woolmer has paid more attention to the one-day game than to test matches," wrote Barlow. "We all know it is an easier game to do well in, in a short space of time.
"Is the national academy the right vehicle? Can it be improved? Is it structured correctly? Is it providing the right players?

"An area that most are loathe to touch upon is affirmative action and the development programme. Every time I attempt to discuss it," wrote Barlow, "I am told that that is the policy. There is nothing to discuss. I recall being told the same thing a couple of years ago -- by the National Party telling me that apartheid was the policy.
"My concern is the amount of money being poured into it with little or no return," concluded Barlow.
The final talking point among South Africans was the reverse sweep played by 20-year-old Paul Adams to the eighth ball he received from Shane Warne. He was caught by Mark Taylor at slip for one.
"I was horrified to see (that shot). Sorry Paul, you looked like a clown," wrote Barlow.
Woolmer admitted after the match that he had asked Adams not to play the shot.

"He is still learning and shouldn't be criticised too harshly," said an editorial in Adams's home town Cape Times. "Of course he should do as the coach says, but is it right to heap all the blame on the number 11 batsman when numbers one to six are consistently failing?"
But if South African fans, in general, have now accepted the tourists as wiser and better over five days, they refuse to concede the honours in the one-day game.
"Give us some coloured clothes and a couple of white balls and we can beat anyone, anytime," said 32-year-old Clubhouse regular Ted Docherty.
